title: A Group of Friends Went to a Phuket Café. Only Four Walked Out Alive.
excerpt: The mysterious death of 26-year-old Kushagra Agarwal after four Indian tourists collapsed simultaneously at a Thai café has rattled the diaspora’s favourite Southeast Asian destination.
body:
It was supposed to be a holiday. A group of five young Indian men at a café near Kamala Beach in Phuket, Thailand’s glittering resort island, enjoying a Saturday night out. By 2:30 AM on May 9, four of them had collapsed. By the time paramedics arrived, one — 26-year-old Kushagra Agarwal — was beyond saving.

The incident, which Thai police are still investigating, has sent a chill through one of the Indian diaspora’s most beloved international destinations. Thailand welcomed over 2.1 million Indian visitors in 2024, and Phuket — with its visa-on-arrival convenience, direct flights from Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru, and a well-established Indian food scene — is often the first international trip for young Indian professionals.

## What Happened

According to witnesses and café staff, the four men showed no signs of distress before suddenly experiencing severe symptoms nearly simultaneously. All four lost consciousness within minutes. Emergency responders from Phuket’s Tourist Police and local rescue teams performed CPR on scene before rushing the victims to hospital. Agarwal was pronounced dead shortly after arrival. The remaining three survivors were initially in serious condition but have since stabilised.

Thai authorities have ordered a full forensic investigation and autopsy. The leading theories under investigation include carbon monoxide poisoning from faulty ventilation or air conditioning units, contaminated food or drink, and recent chemical cleaning or pest control treatments in the café. Local police have stated there were no signs of foul play.

The café has been temporarily closed while health inspectors and forensic teams sweep the premises. Toxicology results are expected within days.

## The Indian Embassy’s Response

The Indian Embassy in Bangkok was notified immediately and has been coordinating with Thai authorities to assist the survivors and arrange the repatriation of Agarwal’s remains. In a statement, the embassy urged Indian tourists in Phuket to “stay vigilant and report any suspicious odours or feelings of sudden dizziness while in enclosed public spaces.”

## What NRI Travellers Should Know

The Phuket incident — while still unexplained — highlights gaps in the safety net that many young Indian travellers take for granted when visiting Southeast Asia.

**Travel insurance is non-negotiable.** Many Indian tourists travel to Thailand without adequate coverage, relying on the low cost of Thai healthcare. But emergency medical evacuation to India can cost ₹15–25 lakh, and repatriation of remains even more. A comprehensive travel insurance policy — not the ₹500 add-on at the airport counter — is essential.

**Know your emergency numbers.** Thailand’s Tourist Police hotline is 1155 and operates in English. Save it before you land. The Indian Embassy’s emergency number in Bangkok is +66-81-837-3353.

**Trust your instincts indoors.** If you feel lightheaded, notice unusual odours, or experience sudden nausea in an enclosed space — a café, bar, hotel room, or massage parlour — leave immediately and get to fresh air. Carbon monoxide is odourless, but the early symptoms (headache, dizziness, nausea) are your body’s alarm system.

**Register with the embassy.** The Indian government’s MADAD portal (madad.gov.in) allows citizens to register their travel plans. In a crisis, this helps consular staff locate and assist you faster.

## A Broader Pattern

This is not the first time Indian tourists have faced medical emergencies in Southeast Asia. The combination of heat, unfamiliar food, alcohol, and poorly ventilated venues creates a cocktail of risk that is easy to underestimate when you are on holiday and in a celebratory mood.

For Agarwal’s family and friends, a Saturday night in paradise became something unimaginable. For the rest of us, it is a reminder that the cheapest part of any international trip should be the insurance — not the afterthought.
